name: North-South Choke
description: Master the North-South Choke in BJJ. Blood choke setup from North-South position. Success rates: Beginner 30%, Intermediate 50%, Advanced 65%.
overview:
The North-South Choke is a devastating blood choke executed from the North-South position, targeting both carotid arteries simultaneously through precise arm positioning and chest pressure. This technique exemplifies the principle of using body weight and structural alignment rather than muscular effort to create submission pressure. The choke becomes available when controlling an opponent from North-South, particularly when they focus on defending arm attacks or attempting to create space.

Strategically, the North-South Choke serves as a powerful complement to Kimura and Americana attacks from North-South position. When opponents defend these arm locks by keeping their elbows tight and hands connected, they often expose their neck to the choke setup. This creates a potent submission dilemma where defending one attack opens vulnerability to another. The technique is particularly effective in no-gi grappling where the lack of collar grips makes traditional chokes difficult.

The key mechanical principle involves threading your choking arm deep under the opponent's neck while your chest drops onto their face, sealing the choke on both sides simultaneously. Unlike collar chokes that can stall or allow breathing, a properly applied North-South Choke produces unconsciousness within seconds due to bilateral carotid compression. This makes it one of the most efficient blood chokes in grappling when executed correctly.
key_principles: Thread choking arm deep under opponent's neck before dropping chest weight
Use chest pressure on opponent's face to seal the far-side carotid artery
Keep hips low and sprawled to prevent opponent from creating space or escaping
Squeeze elbows together rather than pulling with arm strength alone
Position your ear against opponent's chest to maximize choking arm depth
Maintain constant downward pressure throughout the submission attempt
Recognize when opponent is defending arms tightly as the ideal entry window
setup_requirements: Established North-South control with chest-to-chest pressure
Opponent's arms defended or pinned, exposing the neck
Your hips low and sprawled to prevent opponent's hip escape
Head positioned on one side of opponent's body with choking arm threading under neck
Ability to drop full body weight onto opponent's upper body

execution_steps.description: From side control or Kesa Gatame, transition to North-South by walking your body toward opponent's head while maintaining chest pressure. Your chest should be heavy on their upper chest and face.
execution_steps.timing: Execute when opponent defends arm attacks or when transitioning from side control

execution_steps.description: Pin opponent's near arm with your hip or trap it against your body. Their far arm should be controlled by your non-choking arm pressing down on their bicep or elbow to prevent framing.
Slide your choking arm deep under opponent's neck from the side, threading until your bicep is positioned directly under their chin. Your forearm wraps around the far side of their neck.
execution_steps.timing: When opponent's arms are controlled and neck is exposed

execution_steps.description: Drop your ear to opponent's chest on the choking arm side. This maximizes the depth of your arm under their neck and creates the proper angle for bilateral carotid compression.
Drop your chest weight onto opponent's face and upper chest. Your sternum should press against their jaw and cheek, sealing the far-side carotid while your bicep compresses the near-side.

Squeeze your elbows together while maintaining chest pressure and sprawled hips. The compression comes from the structural squeeze of your arms and chest, not from muscular pulling. Hold until tap or unconsciousness.

common_counters.counter: Opponent bridges and creates space before arm is threaded deep enough
common_counters.your_response: Sprawl hips immediately and re-establish chest pressure before reattempting the choke

common_counters.counter: Opponent frames against your hip and shrimps to recover guard
common_counters.your_response: Pin their framing arm with your hip weight and transition to Kimura attack on that arm

common_counters.counter: Opponent turns into you and attempts to take your back
common_counters.your_response: Maintain heavy chest pressure and switch to front headlock control or guillotine setup

common_counters.counter: Opponent tucks chin and blocks arm from threading under neck
common_counters.your_response: Attack Americana or Kimura to force their arms to move, then return to choke when neck opens

common_errors.error: Threading choking arm before establishing proper North-South control
common_errors.consequence: Opponent escapes easily because there is no weight holding them in place during the setup
common_errors.correction: Establish heavy chest pressure and control opponent's arms before beginning the choke sequence

common_errors.error: Keeping hips too high during the choke attempt
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can bridge, create space, and either escape or recover guard
common_errors.correction: Sprawl your hips low to the mat throughout the entire submission attempt

common_errors.error: Relying on arm strength rather than structural squeeze
common_errors.consequence: Fatigue sets in quickly and the choke lacks sufficient pressure to finish
common_errors.correction: Focus on squeezing elbows together and using chest weight rather than pulling with biceps

common_errors.error: Head positioned too far from opponent's body
common_errors.consequence: Choking arm cannot thread deep enough under neck for proper carotid compression
common_errors.correction: Drop your ear directly onto opponent's chest to maximize arm depth under their neck

common_errors.error: Failing to control opponent's arms before attempting choke
common_errors.consequence: Opponent frames effectively and prevents you from dropping weight or threading arm
common_errors.correction: Pin near arm with hip, control far arm with your free hand before committing to choke

common_errors.error: Releasing chest pressure when squeezing for the finish
common_errors.consequence: One carotid artery remains open, allowing blood flow and preventing unconsciousness
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant chest pressure on opponent's face throughout the squeeze

training_progressions.description: Practice transitioning to North-South and threading the choking arm without resistance. Focus on proper head placement with ear on chest and getting maximum depth under opponent's neck. Drill the positional mechanics slowly with a compliant partner.

Add light resistance while developing the squeeze mechanics. Practice maintaining sprawled hips while squeezing elbows together. Partner provides feedback on choke tightness. Begin timing the choke to understand how quickly it takes effect.

Chain the North-South Choke with Kimura and Americana attacks. When partner defends arms, attack choke. When partner defends choke, attack arms. Develop the submission dilemma from North-South position against moderate resistance.

Implement in positional sparring starting from side control or North-South. Focus on recognizing when opponents create the opening for the choke by defending arm attacks. Test against fully resisting partners of varying skill levels.

variants_and_adaptations.description: When opponent keeps their near arm tight, trap it inside the choke along with their neck. This variation can increase pressure but requires proper arm positioning to avoid weakening the choke.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent refuses to move their arm despite Kimura threats

variants_and_adaptations.description: Begin with a paper cutter choke grip from side control, then transition to North-South while maintaining the choking grip. Combines the finishing mechanics of both chokes for enhanced pressure.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent survives paper cutter attempt and you need to increase pressure

variants_and_adaptations.description: Without gi grips, use a gable grip or S-grip behind opponent's head to reinforce the choking arm. Clasp hands together under their neck for additional squeezing power.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: In no-gi grappling where you need extra grip security

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the primary goal of the North-South Choke?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The primary goal is bilateral carotid artery compression, cutting off blood flow to the brain from both sides simultaneously. This is achieved through the combination of your bicep compressing one carotid while your chest pressure seals the other side. Unlike air chokes that restrict breathing, this blood choke produces unconsciousness within seconds when applied correctly.

knowledge_assessment.question: What position do you ideally start the North-South Choke from?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The technique is executed from North-South position, though you can transition there from side control, Kesa Gatame, or other top positions. The key is establishing heavy chest-to-chest pressure with your body perpendicular to your opponent, head-to-head, before threading the choking arm.

knowledge_assessment.question: Where should your head be positioned during the choke?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Your ear should be pressed against your opponent's chest on the same side as your choking arm. This positioning maximizes the depth you can thread your arm under their neck while creating the proper angle for compression. If your head is too far from their body, your arm cannot get deep enough to close both carotids.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent is defending your Kimura attempt by keeping their elbows tight - how does this create an opportunity?
knowledge_assessment.answer: When opponents defend arm attacks by keeping elbows pinned to their sides with hands connected, they expose their neck while occupying their arms defensively. This is the ideal time to transition to the North-South Choke because their arms are occupied and cannot frame against your chest or block your arm from threading under their neck.

knowledge_assessment.question: How do you generate choking pressure without exhausting yourself?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The choke relies on structural pressure rather than muscular effort. Drop your body weight through your chest onto opponent's face, sprawl your hips low, and squeeze your elbows together using skeletal alignment. The compression comes from the structural configuration of your body, not from pulling with your biceps. You should be able to hold the position indefinitely without fatigue.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent starts bridging as you attempt to thread your choking arm - what is your response?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Immediately sprawl your hips hard to the mat and drive your chest weight down onto their face and upper chest. Do not continue trying to thread the arm while they are bridging. Re-establish control first by killing their hip movement with your sprawl, then reattempt the choking arm thread once they are flat and controlled again.

knowledge_assessment.question: What defensive mechanism should you watch for that indicates the choke is not properly sealed?
knowledge_assessment.answer: If your opponent remains conscious and calm after several seconds of squeeze, one or both carotids are not fully compressed. Check that your chest is pressing firmly on their face to seal the far-side carotid, and that your bicep is deep enough under their chin to compress the near-side. A properly sealed North-South Choke produces visible distress and unconsciousness within 5-10 seconds.

knowledge_assessment.question: How do you chain the North-South Choke with arm attacks to create a submission dilemma?
knowledge_assessment.answer: From North-South, attack Kimura on the near arm. When opponent defends by keeping elbows tight and connecting hands, their neck becomes exposed for the choke. If they open their arms to defend the choke, immediately return to the Kimura. This back-and-forth creates a dilemma where defending one attack opens the other, forcing them to give up something.

knowledge_assessment.question: What distinguishes a North-South Choke from a standard arm triangle in terms of mechanics?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The North-South Choke uses your chest weight on opponent's face to seal one carotid while your bicep seals the other. The arm triangle uses opponent's own shoulder as part of the choking structure. In North-South Choke, both compression points come from your body alone, making it effective regardless of opponent's arm position once your arm is threaded deep enough.

knowledge_assessment.question: When should you abandon the North-South Choke attempt and transition to another attack?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Abandon the attempt if opponent successfully creates significant space through bridging or hip escape, if they get strong frames against your body that prevent you from dropping weight, or if they begin turning into you in a way that threatens back exposure. Transition to Kimura, Americana, or re-establish side control rather than forcing a compromised choke position.

safety_considerations: The North-South Choke is a blood choke that can produce unconsciousness within seconds when properly applied. Always train with a partner who understands the tap signal and will tap early during practice. Release immediately upon feeling the tap or seeing any signs of unconsciousness such as body going limp or face changing color. Never hold a blood choke after your partner has gone unconscious in training. When drilling, apply gradually increasing pressure so your partner can tap before full compression. This choke should not be practiced at full intensity without proper supervision and should never be used on training partners who are inexperienced with blood chokes.
position_integration: The North-South Choke integrates into the North-South control system as a primary submission threat that complements arm attacks. From side control or Kesa Gatame, transitioning to North-South opens the submission dilemma between Kimura, Americana, and the North-South Choke. Opponents who successfully defend must expend significant energy, and their defensive reactions often open alternative attacks. When the choke fails, you maintain North-South control and can continue attacking arms or transition to other dominant positions like mount via knee-on-belly. The position also connects to front headlock attacks if opponent turns into you during escape attempts.
